claim: The lateral habenula (LHb) is an epithalamic brain structure critical for processing and adapting to negative action outcomes.
source: The lateral habenula (LHb) is an epithalamic brain structure critical for processing and adapting to negative action outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific understanding of LHb function.

claim: The habenula is divided into medial (MHb) and lateral (LHb) subregions.
source: The habenula is an epithalamic structure divided into medial (MHb) and lateral (LHb) subregions that receives diverse input from the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, basal forebrain, hypothalamus and other regions involved in processing both sensory information and internal state (Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Yetnikoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The habenula receives diverse input from the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, basal forebrain, hypothalamus and other regions involved in processing both sensory information and internal state.
source: The habenula is an epithalamic structure divided into medial (MHb) and lateral (LHb) subregions that receives diverse input from the basal ganglia, frontal cortex, basal forebrain, hypothalamus and other regions involved in processing both sensory information and internal state (Herkenham and Nauta, 1977; Yetnikoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Two main targets of the LHb output are the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and raphe nuclei (dorsal (DRN) and medial (MRN)).
source: Two main targets of the LHb output are major monoaminergic structures in the brain, the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and raphe nuclei (dorsal (DRN) and medial (MRN)), whereas the MHb targets the interpeduncular nucleus (Herkenham and Nauta, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The MHb targets the interpeduncular nucleus.
source: Two main targets of the LHb output are major monoaminergic structures in the brain, the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and raphe nuclei (dorsal (DRN) and medial (MRN)), whereas the MHb targets the interpeduncular nucleus (Herkenham and Nauta, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: LHb has been proposed to contribute to the neurobiological underpinnings of depression and addiction.
source: Due to its dual effects on dopamine and serotonin-producing neurons, LHb has been proposed to contribute to the neurobiological underpinnings of depression and addiction (Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Maroteaux and Mameli, 2012; Meye et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The LHb has dual effects on dopamine and serotonin-producing neurons.
source: Due to its dual effects on dopamine and serotonin-producing neurons, LHb has been proposed to contribute to the neurobiological underpinnings of depression and addiction (Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Maroteaux and Mameli, 2012; Meye et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LHb has been implicated in reward prediction error, aversion, cognition, and adaptive decision making.
source: Furthermore, the LHb has been implicated in a wide range of functions and behaviors including reward prediction error, aversion, cognition, and adaptive decision making (Hikosaka, 2010; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2007; Mizumori and Baker, 2017; Proulx et al., 2014; Tian and Uchida, 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The effects of LHb on each downstream structure and its contribution to different behaviors are likely carried out by distinct populations of neurons.
source: The effects of LHb on each downstream structure and its contribution to different behaviors are likely carried out by distinct populations of neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on logical inference from known LHb functions.

claim: The LHb may, at the macroscopic level, consist of distinct sub-domains with differential contributions to limbic and motor functions.
source: In addition, the LHb may, at the macroscopic level, consist of distinct sub-domains with differential contributions to limbic and motor functions (Zahm and Root, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Habenular neurons show differences in gene expression across hemispheres.
source: Further, many studies suggest that habenular neurons show differences in gene expression across hemispheres (Concha and Wilson, 2001; Pandey et al., 2018), projection targets (Quina et al., 2015), and anatomical location (Gonçalves et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Habenular neurons show differences in gene expression based on projection targets.
source: Further, many studies suggest that habenular neurons show differences in gene expression across hemispheres (Concha and Wilson, 2001; Pandey et al., 2018), projection targets (Quina et al., 2015), and anatomical location (Gonçalves et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Habenular neurons show differences in gene expression based on anatomical location.
source: Further, many studies suggest that habenular neurons show differences in gene expression across hemispheres (Concha and Wilson, 2001; Pandey et al., 2018), projection targets (Quina et al., 2015), and anatomical location (Gonçalves et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The systematic relationship between molecular profiles, projections patterns, and anatomical organization of neurons in the LHb is unknown.
source: Nevertheless, the systematic relationship between molecular profiles, projections patterns, and anatomical organization of neurons in the LHb is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement of the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: The study provides a comprehensive description of the neuronal subtypes in the LHb based on single-cell transcriptional profiling, multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), and cell-type-specific monosynaptic retrograde tracing.
source: Here, we provide a comprehensive description of the neuronal subtypes in the LHb based on single-cell transcriptional profiling, multiplexed fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), and cell-type-specific monosynaptic retrograde tracing.
evidence: This is a statement of the methods and scope of the study.

claim: The MHb has five transcriptionally defined neuronal subtypes.
source: We find that the MHb has five, and LHb has four, transcriptionally defined neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The LHb has four transcriptionally defined neuronal subtypes.
source: We find that the MHb has five, and LHb has four, transcriptionally defined neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on single-cell transcriptional profiling data.

claim: The HbX subtype, which lies at the border between the MHb and LHb, is more transcriptionally similar to other LHb subtypes than MHb subtypes.
source: Interestingly, the HbX subtype, which lies at the border between the MHb and LHb, is more transcriptionally similar to other LHb subtypes than MHb subtypes.
evidence: This is a finding based on analysis of transcriptional data.

claim: The four LHb neuronal subtypes are distinct.
source: We find that the four LHb neuronal subtypes are distinct and monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that they differentially target the dopaminergic and GABAergic neurons of the VTA, as well as the dorsal raphe nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding based on transcriptional profiling and FISH data.

claim: The four LHb neuronal subtypes differentially target the dopaminergic and GABAergic neurons of the VTA.
source: We find that the four LHb neuronal subtypes are distinct and monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that they differentially target the dopaminergic and GABAergic neurons of the VTA, as well as the dorsal raphe nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding based on monosynaptic retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The four LHb neuronal subtypes differentially target the dorsal raphe nucleus.
source: We find that the four LHb neuronal subtypes are distinct and monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that they differentially target the dopaminergic and GABAergic neurons of the VTA, as well as the dorsal raphe nucleus.
evidence: This is a finding based on retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The LHb is organized into subregions defined by transcriptionally discriminable neuronal subtypes.
source: Furthermore, we find the LHb is organized into subregions defined by these transcriptionally discriminable neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is a finding based on FISH and transcriptional profiling data.

claim: Different neuronal classes in the LHb are biased in their projection targets.
source: Together we identify previously unknown neuronal heterogeneity in the habenula and reveal that different neuronal classes are biased in their projection targets.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on retrograde tracing data.

claim: Cell suspensions from the habenula were generated from acute, microdissected brain slices from adult mice, producing 25,289 single-cell transcriptomes (SCTs).
source: Cell suspensions from the habenula were generated from acute, microdissected brain slices from adult mice (Figure 1A), producing 25,289 single-cell transcriptomes (SCTs).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and data collection, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Excluding SCTs with <200 genes, <500 UMIs, or >10% mitochondrial genes resulted in 7,506 SCTs that were further analyzed.
source: Excluding SCTs with <200 genes,<500 UMIs, or >10% mitochondrial genes resulted in 7,506 SCTs that were further analyzed.
evidence: This describes the quality control filtering applied to the data.

claim: The filtered dataset had median counts of 2593 UMIs (min = 501, max = 17787, IQR = 3986) and 349 genes (min = 302, max = 5276, IQR = 1733) per cell.
source: This subset had median counts of 2593 UMIs (min = 501, max = 17787, IQR = 3986) and 349 genes (min = 302, max = 5276, IQR = 1733) per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the filtered dataset, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Analysis of gene expression patterns by principal components (PC) analysis and shared-nearest-neighbors resulted in 12 cellular clusters.
source: Subsequent analysis of gene expression patterns by principal components (PC) analysis and shared-nearest-neighbors (Satija et al., 2015) resulted in 12 cellular clusters (Figure 1B, see Materials and methods for details on sequential clustering).
evidence: This describes the clustering analysis performed on the data, with reference to Figure 1B and a citation to the method.

claim: Major cell classes within the 12 clusters were identified by expression of cell-type-specific gene combinations that were extensively cross-referenced with published datasets.
source: Major cell classes (i.e. neurons, astrocytes, microglia, etc…) within these clusters were identified by expression of cell-type-specific gene combinations that were extensive cross-referenced with published datasets (Saunders et al., 2018; Zeisel et al., 2018) (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This describes the method for identifying cell types, with citations to published datasets and reference to Figure 1B-C.

claim: The data confirmed recent work on non-neuronal cell-types in habenula describing high levels of Tnf in microphages and microglia.
source: Our data confirmed recent work on non-neuronal cell-types in habenula describing high levels of Tnf in microphages and microglia (Valentinova et al., 2019) and high levels of Kir4.1 (Kcnj10) in astrocytes (Cui et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a validation of the data against prior published work, with citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The data confirmed recent work on non-neuronal cell-types in habenula describing high levels of Kir4.1 (Kcnj10) in astrocytes.
source: Our data confirmed recent work on non-neuronal cell-types in habenula describing high levels of Tnf in microphages and microglia (Valentinova et al., 2019) and high levels of Kir4.1 (Kcnj10) in astrocytes (Cui et al., 2018) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a validation of the data against prior published work, with citations and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In contrast to other species, no major transcriptional differences were observed across left and right hemispheres in the mouse habenula.
source: In contrast to other species (Pandey et al., 2018), no major transcriptional differences were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) across left and right hemispheres; therefore, cells from both hemispheres were pooled for analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with a citation to work in other species and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Cells from both hemispheres were pooled for analysis.
source: In contrast to other species (Pandey et al., 2018), no major transcriptional differences were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B) across left and right hemispheres; therefore, cells from both hemispheres were pooled for analysis.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision based on the data analysis.

claim: The majority of the cells in the dataset were neurons (53%).
source: The majority of the cells in the dataset were neurons (53%) and we focused our analysis on these clusters for the remainder of the study.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the cell type composition in the dataset.

claim: Neurons (n = 3,930 cells) were identified by expression of genes required for chemical synaptic transmission such as Snap25, Syp, and Syt4.
source: Neurons (n = 3,930 cells), identified by expression of genes required for chemical synaptic transmission such as Snap25, Syp, and Syt4, clustered into two main classes (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying neurons in the dataset, with reference to Figure 1B-C.

claim: Neurons clustered into two main classes.
source: Neurons (n = 3,930 cells), identified by expression of genes required for chemical synaptic transmission such as Snap25, Syp, and Syt4, clustered into two main classes (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, with reference to Figure 1B-C.

claim: The larger cluster of neurons (n = 3,370 cells) expressed Tac2 and corresponds to the MHb.
source: The larger cluster of neurons (n = 3,370 cells) expressed Tac2 and corresponds to the MHb (Figure 2), whereas the smaller cluster (n = 560 cells) expressed Gap43 and corresponds to the LHb (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding based on differential gene expression and ISH data, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The smaller cluster of neurons (n = 560 cells) expressed Gap43 and corresponds to the LHb.
source: The larger cluster of neurons (n = 3,370 cells) expressed Tac2 and corresponds to the MHb (Figure 2), whereas the smaller cluster (n = 560 cells) expressed Gap43 and corresponds to the LHb (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding based on differential gene expression and ISH data, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Tac2 expression is restricted to cells in the MHb.
source: Location of MHb and ISH of Tac2 expression from the Allen Institute Database. Tac2 expression is restricted to cells in the MHb in this region.
evidence: This is a finding from ISH data from the Allen Institute Database, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tac2 serves as an excellent marker for MHb neurons in the dataset of SCTs.
source: Tac2 serves as an excellent marker for MHb neurons in the dataset of SCTs (Scale on right shows normalized (log) gene expression.)
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the gene expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Analysis of MHb neurons revealed that they could be divided into eight clusters.
source: Analysis of MHb neurons revealed that they could be divided into eight clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three MHb clusters were clearly distinguished by high expression of activity-dependent genes (ADGs).
source: However, three clusters were clearly distinguished by high expression of activity-dependent genes (ADGs) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that they might simply reflect neurons of other clusters that had been recently strongly activated.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Regressing out the PC containing a large number of ADGs caused the three high ADG clusters to merge with other MHb clusters, leaving five distinct subtypes of MHb neurons.
source: Indeed, regressing out the PC containing a large number of ADGs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F) caused these three high ADGs clusters to merge with other MHb clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D), leaving five distinct subtypes of MHb neurons.
evidence: This describes a data processing step and its result, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: All MHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and Slc17a7, the genes encoding vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2.
source: All MHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and Slc17a7, the genes encoding vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2, and Tac2 suggesting that all MHb neurons are glutamatergic and produce the neuropeptide Neurokinin B (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: All MHb neurons expressed high levels of Tac2.
source: All MHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and Slc17a7, the genes encoding vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2, and Tac2 suggesting that all MHb neurons are glutamatergic and produce the neuropeptide Neurokinin B (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: All MHb neurons are glutamatergic and produce the neuropeptide Neurokinin B.
source: All MHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and Slc17a7, the genes encoding vesicular glutamate transporters 1 and 2, and Tac2 suggesting that all MHb neurons are glutamatergic and produce the neuropeptide Neurokinin B (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two of the five MHb clusters also expressed Slc18a3 and Chat, the vesicular transporter and biosynthetic enzyme for acetylcholine, respectively.
source: Two of the five clusters also expressed Slc18a3 and Chat (not shown), the vesicular transporter and biosynthetic enzyme for acetylcholine, respectively, indicating that these neurons may co-release glutamate and acetylcholine (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), as has been described in several studies (Ren et al., 2011; Soria-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two MHb clusters may co-release glutamate and acetylcholine.
source: Two of the five clusters also expressed Slc18a3 and Chat (not shown), the vesicular transporter and biosynthetic enzyme for acetylcholine, respectively, indicating that these neurons may co-release glutamate and acetylcholine (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), as has been described in several studies (Ren et al., 2011; Soria-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data and supported by citations to prior research, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: No MHb neurons expressed significant levels of the canonical GABA handling genes Slc32a1, Gad1, or Slc18a2.
source: Interestingly, no MHb neurons expressed significant levels of the canonical GABA handling genes Slc32a1, Gad1, or Slc18a2 (although Gad2 was expressed at low levels in all subtypes); therefore, they are unlikely to release GABA.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data.

claim: Gad2 was expressed at low levels in all MHb subtypes.
source: Interestingly, no MHb neurons expressed significant levels of the canonical GABA handling genes Slc32a1, Gad1, or Slc18a2 (although Gad2 was expressed at low levels in all subtypes); therefore, they are unlikely to release GABA.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data.

claim: MHb neurons are unlikely to release GABA.
source: Interestingly, no MHb neurons expressed significant levels of the canonical GABA handling genes Slc32a1, Gad1, or Slc18a2 (although Gad2 was expressed at low levels in all subtypes); therefore, they are unlikely to release GABA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of key GABA-related genes in the expression data.

claim: Individual DEGs for particular MHb subtypes consistently mapped onto discrete regions in the MHb.
source: Generally, we found that individual DEGs for particular MHb subtypes consistently mapped onto discrete regions in the MHb (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-referencing DEGs with ISH data, with reference to Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DEGs for MHb neurons were rarely DEGs for LHb neurons.
source: Also, DEGs for MHb neurons were rarely DEGs for LHb neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: MHb neurons divided along the dorsal/ventral axis with a third lateral subtype.
source: MHb neurons divided along the dorsal/ventral axis with a third lateral (enriched for genes Sema3d, Calb1, and Spon1) subtype (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs, with reference to Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: The lateral MHb subtype is enriched for genes Sema3d, Calb1, and Spon1.
source: MHb neurons divided along the dorsal/ventral axis with a third lateral (enriched for genes Sema3d, Calb1, and Spon1) subtype (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis, with reference to Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Ventral MHb groups could be further subdivided into two distinct subtypes, the 'ventral two thirds' of the MHb (enriched for Lmo3) and the 'ventrolateral' MHb (enriched for genes Esam and Slc18a3).
source: Ventral groups could be further subdivided into two distinct subtypes, the 'ventral two thirds' of the MHb (enriched for Lmo3) and the 'ventrolateral' MHb (enriched for genes Esam and Slc18a3).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression and spatial mapping analysis.

claim: Gene expression patterns indicated that it is possible that neurons from the 'ventral two thirds' and 'ventrolateral' MHb subtypes were partially intermingled and did not form a defined border.
source: Gene expression patterns indicated that it is possible that neurons from these two subtypes were partially intermingled and did not form a defined border (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of gene expression, with reference to Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The rest of the MHb could be subdivided into the 'dorsal' (enriched for genes Col16a1, Wif1, and Adcyap1) and 'superior' (enriched for genes Cck and Avil) subtypes.
source: The rest of the MHb could be subdivided into the 'dorsal' (enriched for genes Col16a1, Wif1, and Adcyap1) and 'superior' (enriched for genes Cck and Avil) subtypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression and spatial mapping analysis.

claim: The 'dorsal' and 'superior' MHb subtypes split along a medial/lateral axis with the 'dorsal' being more laterally located than the 'superior'.
source: These two groups split along a medial/lateral axis with the 'dorsal' being more laterally located than the 'superior' (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F–I) (Wagner et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs, with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F-I.

claim: Gap43 is highly expressed in the LHb.
source: Gap43 is highly expressed in the LHb and along with several other genes (Htr2c, Pcdh10, Gabra1, and Syn2) distinguishes neurons of this region from those of neighboring MHb (Figure 3A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 3A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gap43, along with several other genes (Htr2c, Pcdh10, Gabra1, and Syn2), distinguishes LHb neurons from those of neighboring MHb.
source: Gap43 is highly expressed in the LHb and along with several other genes (Htr2c, Pcdh10, Gabra1, and Syn2) distinguishes neurons of this region from those of neighboring MHb (Figure 3A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the differential gene expression analysis, with reference to Figure 3A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unlike for MHb neurons, significant elevation of ADGs was not detected in LHb neurons.
source: Unlike for MHb neurons, we did not detect significant elevation of ADGs in LHb neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis.

claim: Four distinct clusters of neurons were found in LHb.
source: We found four distinct clusters of neurons in LHb which, again unlike MHb, did not have distinct expression profiles of genes involved in the synthesis and packaging of different typical fast neurotransmitters (e.g. glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine) – all LHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and very low levels of Slc32a1, suggesting that they are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: LHb neuron clusters did not have distinct expression profiles of genes involved in the synthesis and packaging of different typical fast neurotransmitters.
source: We found four distinct clusters of neurons in LHb which, again unlike MHb, did not have distinct expression profiles of genes involved in the synthesis and packaging of different typical fast neurotransmitters (e.g. glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine) – all LHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and very low levels of Slc32a1, suggesting that they are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis.

claim: All LHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and very low levels of Slc32a1, suggesting that they are glutamatergic.
source: We found four distinct clusters of neurons in LHb which, again unlike MHb, did not have distinct expression profiles of genes involved in the synthesis and packaging of different typical fast neurotransmitters (e.g. glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine) – all LHb neurons expressed high levels of Slc17a6 and very low levels of Slc32a1, suggesting that they are glutamatergic.
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data and an inference about neurotransmitter identity.

claim: DEGs for LHb subtypes showed four distinct, but consistent patterns that aligned with their subclusters.
source: We found that DEGs showed four distinct, but consistent patterns that aligned with their subclusters (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is a finding from cross-referencing DEGs with ISH data, with reference to Figure 3C-D.

claim: One LHb cluster showed high expression of DEGs in both the 'lateral oval' and 'central medial' subdivision, named the oval/medial subdivision.
source: These consisted of 1) a cluster that showed high expression of DEGs in both the 'lateral oval' and 'central medial' subdivision, we named this the oval/medial subdivision;
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs.

claim: One LHb cluster showed high expression of DEGs in the 'marginal subdivision of the medial division of the LHb', called the marginal subdivision.
source: 2) a cluster that showed high expression of DEGs in the 'marginal subdivision of the medial division of the LHb', we called this the marginal subdivision;
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs.

claim: One LHb cluster showed high expression of DEGs in the 'lateral' subdivision (but avoiding expression in the 'lateral oval'), called the lateral subdivision.
source: 3) a cluster that showed high expression of DEGs in the 'lateral' subdivision (but avoiding expression in the 'lateral oval'), we also called this the lateral subdivision;
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs.

claim: One LHb cluster showed high expression of DEGs in the subdivision defined as 'HbX' lying on the dorsal border between MHb and LHb, also referred to as the HbX subdivision.
source: and 4) a cluster that showed high expression of DEGs in the subdivision defined as 'HbX' lying on the dorsal border between MHb and LHb, we also refer to this as the HbX subdivision (Figure 3C) (Wagner et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of DEGs, with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The HbX region is more closely related in its gene expression to other LHb clusters than to any clusters in the MHb.
source: Interestingly, the HbX region is more closely related in its gene expression to other LHb clusters than to any clusters in the MHb; therefore, it is more similar to LHb neurons than previously recognized (Figure 3D) (Wagner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression analysis, with a citation to prior work and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Multiplexed FISH confirmed the four transcriptionally defined clusters of LHb neurons were distinct.
source: We performed multiplexed FISH to confirm the four transcriptionally defined clusters of LHb neurons were distinct and to further examine their spatial organization within the LHb.
evidence: This describes the purpose and result of the FISH experiments.

claim: Four highly expressed DEGs (Chrm3, Vgf, Gpr151, and Sst) were chosen to represent each LHb cluster.
source: We chose four highly expressed DEGs that represented each LHb cluster (Chrm3, Vgf, Gpr151, and Sst) and examined their expression in individual neurons (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: The chosen genes (Chrm3, Vgf, Gpr151, and Sst) generally expressed in different cells, confirming that they defined molecularly distinct neuronal subtypes.
source: As predicted by the single-cell sequencing, the chosen genes generally expressed in different cells, confirming that they defined molecularly distinct neuronal subtypes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Individual neurons in the HbX expressed both Sst and Gpr151.
source: An exception to this general rule, but consistent with the predictions of single-cell sequencing, individual neurons in the HbX expressed both Sst and Gpr151 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: When strongly expressed, Chrm3 and Vgf were found in different cells, but they were occasionally co-expressed in neurons that had relatively low levels of both genes.
source: Additionally, when strongly expressed, Chrm3 and Vgf were found in different cells, but they were occasionally co-expressed in neurons that had relatively low levels of both genes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The chosen genes are largely expressed in non-overlapping patterns at the macroscopic level, confirming the organization of LHb into molecularly defined subregions.
source: The chosen genes are largely expressed in non-overlapping patterns at the macroscopic level, confirming the organization of LHb into molecularly defined subregions (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells expressing DEGs from different LHb subtypes occupied distinct spatial domains along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb.
source: More specifically, cells expressing DEGs from different subtypes occupied distinct spatial domains along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells from a LHb subtype did intermingle with cells of another group and sharply defined borders between LHb subregions were not observed.
source: However, cells from a subtype did intermingle with cells of another group and sharply defined borders between LHb subregions were not observed (e.g. Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of DEGs from the same LHb subgroup overlap both regionally, and in single cells.
source: Multichannel FISH for this second set of genes combined with the previous set confirmed that expression of DEGs from the same subgroup overlap both regionally, and in single cells (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Most of the DEGs did not show obvious gradients in expression along the medial/lateral axis using FISH.
source: Importantly, we did not observe obvious gradients in expression along the medial/lateral axis for most of the DEGs using FISH; however, Plch1 expression did decrease gradually for cells positioned more lateral within the LHb (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Plch1 expression decreased gradually for cells positioned more lateral within the LHb.
source: Importantly, we did not observe obvious gradients in expression along the medial/lateral axis for most of the DEGs using FISH; however, Plch1 expression did decrease gradually for cells positioned more lateral within the LHb (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The LHb projects via the fasciculus retroflexus to the ventral tegmental area (VTA), rostromedial tegmental area (RMTg), and median/dorsal raphe.
source: The LHb projects via the fasciculus retroflexus to the ventral tegmental area (VTA), rostromedial tegmental area (RMTg), and median/dorsal raphe (Herkenham and Nauta, 1977).
evidence: This is a statement of known anatomy supported by a citation.

claim: The VTA consists of a large and diverse population of dopamine neurons, as well as smaller populations of purely GABAergic, purely glutamatergic, and GABA/glutamate coreleasing neurons.
source: The VTA consists of a large and diverse population of dopamine neurons, as well as smaller populations of purely GABAergic, purely glutamatergic, and GABA/glutamate coreleasing neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of known VTA cell type composition.

claim: Both GABAergic and dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input from the LHb.
source: Both GABAergic and dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input from the LHb (Beier et al., 2015; Lammel et al., 2012; Morales and Margolis, 2017; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012) but it is unknown if these arise from molecularly distinct LHb neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of known connectivity supported by citations.

claim: It is unknown if LHb inputs to GABAergic and dopaminergic VTA neurons arise from molecularly distinct LHb neurons.
source: Both GABAergic and dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input from the LHb (Beier et al., 2015; Lammel et al., 2012; Morales and Margolis, 2017; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012) but it is unknown if these arise from molecularly distinct LHb neurons.
evidence: This is a statement of a knowledge gap that motivates the experiments.

claim: Rabies virus-based monosynaptic retrograde tracing was used to test if there was connectivity specificity between LHb and VTA neuronal subtypes.
source: We tested if there was connectivity specificity between LHb and VTA neuronal subtypes using rabies virus-based monosynaptic retrograde tracing (Wickersham et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, with a citation to the method.

claim: Approximately 30% of 'starter cells' in VGAT-IRES-Cre mice coexpressed Slc17a6 (Vglut2) indicating they are likely GABA/glutamate coreleasing neurons.
source: FISH in the VTA revealed that ~ 30% of 'starter cells' (neurons that were GFP+ and Cre+), coexpressed Slc17a6 (Vglut2) indicating they are likely GABA/glutamate coreleasing neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F) (Root et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis of starter cells, with a citation to prior work and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The majority of the remaining 70% of 'starter cells' in VGAT-IRES-Cre mice are purely GABAergic.
source: The majority of the remaining 70% of 'starter cells' are purely GABAergic (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FISH data, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Retrogradely labeled neurons were found in all four LHb subtypes following injections into VGAT-IRES-Cre mice.
source: Using FISH we found retrogradely labeled neurons, marked by expression of RbV-N mRNA, in all four LHb subtypes (identified using enriched genes Chrm3, Vgf, Gpr151, and Sst) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the retrograde tracing and FISH experiments, with reference to Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of retrogradely labeled LHb neurons from VGAT-IRES-Cre VTA injections were found in the lateral and oval/medial subtypes in roughly equal proportions (mean ± SEM: 48 ± 0.5% Gpr151+ and 41 ± 0.6% Chrm3+, respectively).
source: The majority of retrogradely labeled LHb neurons were found in the lateral and oval/medial subtypes in roughly equal proportions (mean ± SEM: 48 ± 0.5% Gpr151+ and 41 ± 0.6% Chrm3+, respectively) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: A much smaller proportion of retrogradely labeled LHb neurons from VGAT-IRES-Cre VTA injections was found in the marginal subtype (10 ± 1% Vgf+).
source: A much smaller proportion was found in the marginal subtype (10 ± 1% Vgf+), and very few HbX neurons (2 ± 1% Sst+) were retrogradely labeled.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: Very few HbX neurons (2 ± 1% Sst+) were retrogradely labeled from VGAT-IRES-Cre VTA injections.
source: A much smaller proportion was found in the marginal subtype (10 ± 1% Vgf+), and very few HbX neurons (2 ± 1% Sst+) were retrogradely labeled.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The distribution of retrogradely labeled cells from VGAT-IRES-Cre VTA injections was skewed laterally along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb.
source: As a population, the distribution of retrogradely labeled cells was skewed laterally along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of retrogradely labeled cells, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 9% of 'starter cells' in DAT-IRES-Cre mice coexpressed Slc32a1 (VGAT) and Slc6a3 (dopamine transporter, DAT) indicating they are dopaminergic neurons that also express Slc32a1.
source: FISH in the VTA revealed that ~9% of 'starter cells' (neurons that were GFP+ and Cre+), coexpressed Slc32a1 (VGAT) and Slc6a3 (dopamine transporter, DAT) indicating they are dopaminergic neurons that also express Slc32a1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G) (Morales and Margolis, 2017; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis of starter cells, with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The remaining 91% of starter cells in DAT-IRES-Cre mice express only Slc6a3 indicating low levels of starter cell overlap with the experiments done in the VGAT-IRES-Cre line.
source: The remaining 91% of starter cells express only Slc6a3 indicating low levels of starter cell overlap with the experiments done in the VGAT-IRES-Cre line (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis of starter cells, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2F.

claim: A much larger proportion of retrogradely labeled neurons in the oval/medial and marginal subtypes (61 ± 2% Chrm3+ and 20 ± 1% Vgf+, respectively) were found in the DAT-IRES-Cre than the VGAT-IRES-Cre line.
source: We performed FISH on retrogradely labeled neurons in the LHb and found that a much larger proportion of retrogradely labeled neurons in the oval/medial and marginal subtypes (61 ± 2% Chrm3+ and 20 ± 1% Vgf+, respectively) in the DAT-IRES-Cre than the VGAT-IRES-Cre line (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5B-D.

claim: A smaller proportion of neurons in the lateral subtype were labeled in DAT-IRES-Cre mice (10 ± 0.4% Gpr151+) compared to VGAT-IRES-Cre mice.
source: Consequently, a smaller proportion of neurons in the lateral subtype were labeled (10 ± 0.4% Gpr151+) and almost no neurons in the HbX subregion were labeled (0.7 ± 0.5% Sst+) (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Almost no neurons in the HbX subregion were labeled in DAT-IRES-Cre mice (0.7 ± 0.5% Sst+).
source: Consequently, a smaller proportion of neurons in the lateral subtype were labeled (10 ± 0.4% Gpr151+) and almost no neurons in the HbX subregion were labeled (0.7 ± 0.5% Sst+) (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The retrogradely labeled cells from injections into DAT-IRES-Cre mice were distributed relatively evenly along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb.
source: In contrast to the results from injections into VGAT-IRES-Cre mice, the retrogradely labeled cells from injections into DAT-IRES-Cre mice were distributed relatively evenly along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of retrogradely labeled cells, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons can receive input from all four subtypes of LHb neuron.
source: Together these data suggest that both VTA GABAergic and dopaminergic neurons can receive input from all four subtypes of LHb neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the retrograde tracing data.

claim: VTA dopaminergic neurons receive the largest proportion of their LHb input from the oval/medial LHb subtype.
source: However, VTA dopaminergic neurons receive the largest proportion of their LHb input from the oval/medial LHb subtype, whereas VTA GABAergic neurons receive equal levels of input from both the oval/medial and lateral LHb subtypes (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: VTA GABAergic neurons receive equal levels of input from both the oval/medial and lateral LHb subtypes.
source: However, VTA dopaminergic neurons receive the largest proportion of their LHb input from the oval/medial LHb subtype, whereas VTA GABAergic neurons receive equal levels of input from both the oval/medial and lateral LHb subtypes (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: The LHb input to VTA GABAergic neurons is skewed laterally in the LHb, while input to dopamine neurons is evenly distributed along the medial/lateral axis.
source: Furthermore, the LHb input to VTA GABAergic neurons is skewed laterally in the LHb, while input to dopamine neurons is evenly distributed along the medial/lateral axis (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial analysis of retrograde tracing data, with reference to Figure 5B-C.

claim: LHb neurons heavily innervate the dorsal and median raphe nuclei (DRN/MRN) and modulate serotonergic output throughout the brain.
source: LHb neurons heavily innervate the dorsal and median raphe nuclei (DRN/MRN) and modulate serotonergic output throughout the brain (Zhao et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of known connectivity and function supported by citations.

claim: A non-pseudotyped G-deleted rabies virus (RbV-GFP) was injected into the DRN to examine the LHb subtypes that project to the DRN.
source: To examine the LHb subtypes that project to the DRN, we injected a non-pseudotyped G-deleted rabies virus (RbV-GFP) into this area and performed FISH in the LHb for subtype enriched genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Non-pseudotyped G-deleted rabies virus does infect axons but does not spread across synapses formed onto the infected cell due to deletion of the rabies glycoprotein (G).
source: Importantly, non-pseudotyped G-deleted rabies virus does infect axons but does not spread across synapses formed onto the infected cell due to deletion of the rabies glycoprotein (G).
evidence: This is a description of the properties of the virus used, based on established knowledge.

claim: Similar to dopaminergic VTA neurons, the DRN received the largest proportion of its LHb input from the oval/medial subtype (51 ± 2% Chrm3+).
source: Similar to dopaminergic VTA neurons, the DRN received the largest proportion of its LHb input from the oval/medial subtype (51 ± 2% Chrm3+) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The DRN also received minor inputs from the lateral (16 ± 5% Gpr151+), marginal (28 ± 5% Vgf+), and HbX (1 ± 0.5% Sst+) regions.
source: The DRN also received minor inputs from the lateral (16 ± 5% Gpr151+), marginal (28 ± 5% Vgf+), and HbX (1 ± 0.5% Sst+) regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The proportions of input to the DRN arising from different LHb subtypes were more similar to those to VTA dopamine neurons than those to VTA GABA neurons.
source: Overall, the proportions of input to the DRN arising from different LHb subtypes were more similar to those to VTA dopamine neurons than those to VTA GABA neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of the quantitative retrograde tracing data, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and Supplementary file 6.

claim: The distribution of LHb input to DRN has a prominent spike on the medial edge of the LHb indicating that large proportion of the LHb input to DRN is located in this area.
source: However, the distribution of LHb input to DRN has a prominent spike on the medial edge of the LHb indicating that large proportion of the LHb input to DRN is located in this area (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of retrogradely labeled cells, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and D.

claim: The LHb neurons are grossly organized along the medial/lateral axis based on their projection target: the most medial LHb neurons preferentially target the DRN, whereas the most lateral LHb neurons preferentially target VTA GABA neurons.
source: Therefore, the LHb neurons are grossly organized along the medial/lateral axis based on their projection target: the most medial LHb neurons preferentially target the DRN, whereas the most lateral LHb neurons preferentially target VTA GABA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: Input to VTA DA neurons is distributed relatively evenly along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb.
source: Finally, input to VTA DA neurons is distributed relatively evenly along the medial/lateral axis of the LHb (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial analysis of retrograde tracing data, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The study performed transcriptional and anatomical analyses of the habenula, a crucial circuit node that modifies brain-wide dopamine and serotonin levels through its connections to the VTA and DRN.
source: We performed transcriptional and anatomical analyses of the habenula, a crucial circuit node that modifies brain-wide dopamine and serotonin levels through its connections to the VTA and DRN (Proulx et al., 2014; Tian and Uchida, 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's scope, with citations to prior work.

claim: Using large-scale single-cell transcriptional profiling, the study classifies MHb and LHb neurons into five and four major neuron types, respectively.
source: Using large-scale single-cell transcriptional profiling, we classify MHb and LHb neurons into five and four major neuron types, respectively, and show that each class has a distinct gene expression pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Each class of MHb and LHb neurons has a distinct gene expression pattern.
source: Using large-scale single-cell transcriptional profiling, we classify MHb and LHb neurons into five and four major neuron types, respectively, and show that each class has a distinct gene expression pattern.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The four LHb populations were confirmed to be non-overlapping at the single-cell level by FISH.
source: The four LHb populations were confirmed to be non-overlapping at the single-cell level by FISH.
evidence: This is a summary of the FISH validation experiments.

claim: Monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that GABAergic VTA neurons receive equal input from the oval/medial and lateral LHb neuronal subtypes.
source: Monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that GABAergic VTA neurons receive equal input from the oval/medial and lateral LHb neuronal subtypes, whereas dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input primarily from the oval/medial LHb subtype.
evidence: This is a summary of the retrograde tracing findings.

claim: Dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input primarily from the oval/medial LHb subtype.
source: Monosynaptic retrograde tracing revealed that GABAergic VTA neurons receive equal input from the oval/medial and lateral LHb neuronal subtypes, whereas dopaminergic VTA neurons receive input primarily from the oval/medial LHb subtype.
evidence: This is a summary of the retrograde tracing findings.

claim: Neurons of the DRN receive input from similar LHb cell-types in roughly similar proportions to dopaminergic VTA neurons.
source: Neurons of the DRN receive input from similar LHb cell-types in roughly similar proportions to dopaminergic VTA neurons; however, the LHb cells that target the DRN are skewed medially compared to the cells that target either dopaminergic or GABAergic cells of the VTA.
evidence: This is a summary of the retrograde tracing findings.

claim: The LHb cells that target the DRN are skewed medially compared to the cells that target either dopaminergic or GABAergic cells of the VTA.
source: Neurons of the DRN receive input from similar LHb cell-types in roughly similar proportions to dopaminergic VTA neurons; however, the LHb cells that target the DRN are skewed medially compared to the cells that target either dopaminergic or GABAergic cells of the VTA.
evidence: This is a summary of the retrograde tracing findings.

claim: Recent studies have identified and delineated the subnuclei of the mouse MHb using morphological, topographic and cytochemical criteria.
source: Recent studies have identified and delineated the subnuclei of the mouse MHb using morphological, topographic and cytochemical criteria (Wagner et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations.

claim: The anatomical location of MHb subtypes identified by single-cell transcriptional profiling largely agree with previously defined MHb subnuclei.
source: The anatomical location of these subtypes largely agree with previously defined MHb subnuclei and we have used the same nomenclature when possible (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Wagner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's findings with prior work, with a citation and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two ventral subtypes of the MHb coexpressed transcripts for glutamate and ACh neurotransmission.
source: The two ventral subtypes of the MHb coexpressed transcripts for glutamate and ACh neurotransmission (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The two ventral MHb subtypes can be differentially targeted with intersectional approaches, as genes such as Lmo3 and Esam are preferentially expressed in one subtype.
source: Our data suggest these two ventral subtypes can be differentially targeted with intersectional approaches, as genes such as Lmo3 and Esam are preferentially expressed in one subtype (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Previous studies indicate that MHb neurons that release glutamate and ACh target the medial interpeduncular nucleus (IPN).
source: Previous studies indicate that MHb neurons that release glutamate and ACh target the medial interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) (Ren et al., 2011) and are involved in the formation of aversive memories (Soria-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations.

claim: MHb neurons that release glutamate and ACh are involved in the formation of aversive memories.
source: Previous studies indicate that MHb neurons that release glutamate and ACh target the medial interpeduncular nucleus (IPN) (Ren et al., 2011) and are involved in the formation of aversive memories (Soria-Gómez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Cholinergic transmission in MHb has been implicated in nicotine addiction as MHb neurons not only release ACh, but express an array of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits (nAChRs, such as Chrna3 and Chrnb3).
source: Additionally, cholinergic transmission in MHb has also been implicated in nicotine addiction as MHb neurons not only release ACh, but express an array of nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits (nAChRs, such as Chrna3 and Chrnb3; Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 6) (Fowler et al., 2011; Shih et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 6.

claim: MHb likely plays an important role in mediating the unpleasant symptoms associated with nicotine withdrawal.
source: Similar to its involvement in aversive memories, MHb likely plays an important role in mediating the unpleasant symptoms associated with nicotine withdrawal (Zhao-Shea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The data provide a comprehensive view of all nAChR and mAChR transcripts expressed in both MHb and LHb providing a resource for the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of addiction.
source: Our data provide a comprehensive view of all nAChR and mAChR transcripts expressed in both MHb and LHb providing a resource for the development of new therapeutic targets for the treatment of addiction (Figure 2—figure supplements 6–8) (D'Souza, 2016; Zuo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of the potential utility of the data, with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 2—figure supplements 6-8.

claim: Few studies have examined the function of the dorsal (enriched for genes Col16a1, Wif1, and Adcyap1) and superior (enriched for genes Cck, and Avil) MHb.
source: Few studies have examined the function of the dorsal (enriched for genes Col16a1, Wif1, and Adcyap1) and superior (enriched for genes Cck, and Avil) MHb.
evidence: This is a statement of a knowledge gap.

claim: Dorsal and superior MHb neurons were known to express high levels of Tac1 (the gene that produces the neuropeptide substance P), consistent with the single-cell sequencing data.
source: These neurons were known to express high levels of Tac1 (the gene that produces the neuropeptide substance P), consistent with our single-cell sequencing data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J) and target the lateral IPN (Hsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation, validated by the study's data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: Dorsal and superior MHb neurons target the lateral IPN.
source: These neurons were known to express high levels of Tac1 (the gene that produces the neuropeptide substance P), consistent with our single-cell sequencing data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J) and target the lateral IPN (Hsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of dorsal and superior MHb neurons may be reinforcing.
source: Their activation may be reinforcing (Hsu et al., 2014), but detailed analysis of their function and neurotransmitter release has not been examined.
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The study's map of LHb largely agrees with previous work and adds many key observations into the organization and cellular and molecular diversity of the LHb.
source: Overall, our map largely agrees with previous work and adds many key observations into the organization and cellular and molecular diversity of the LHb.
evidence: This is a summary statement comparing the study's findings to prior work.

claim: The study provides multiple genetic handles that can be used in future studies to target LHb neuron subtypes.
source: In addition to providing multiple genetic handles that can be used in future studies to target LHb neuron subtypes, our study reveals the a wide range of GPCRs (such as Htr2c, Htr5b, Sstr2, Cnr1, Gpr158, Lpar1, Adcyap1r1; see Figure 2—figure supplement 8) expressed in LHb neurons that could be targeted for treatment of diseases known to effect LHb function such as depression, anxiety, and addiction (Lecca et al., 2014; Proulx et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of the potential utility of the data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The study reveals a wide range of GPCRs (such as Htr2c, Htr5b, Sstr2, Cnr1, Gpr158, Lpar1, Adcyap1r1) expressed in LHb neurons that could be targeted for treatment of diseases known to affect LHb function such as depression, anxiety, and addiction.
source: In addition to providing multiple genetic handles that can be used in future studies to target LHb neuron subtypes, our study reveals the a wide range of GPCRs (such as Htr2c, Htr5b, Sstr2, Cnr1, Gpr158, Lpar1, Adcyap1r1; see Figure 2—figure supplement 8) expressed in LHb neurons that could be targeted for treatment of diseases known to effect LHb function such as depression, anxiety, and addiction (Lecca et al., 2014; Proulx et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of the potential utility of the data, with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: In contrast to some reports, the study did not find evidence of GABAergic neurons in the LHb (or MHb).
source: In contrast to some reports (Zhang et al., 2018), we did not find evidence of GABAergic neurons in the LHb (or MHb).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, contrasted with a citation to prior work.

claim: Although Gad2 and Slc6a1 were present at low levels in all LHb clusters, Slc32a1 or Slc18a2, which are required for vesicular loading of GABA, were not found.
source: Although Gad2 and Slc6a1, which encode a GABA synthetic enzyme and GABA transporter, respectively, were present at low levels in all LHb clusters we did not find expression of Slc32a1 or Slc18a2, which are required for vesicular loading of GABA (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data.

claim: Gad2 expression is a poor discriminator for inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons.
source: This is in agreement with recently published results demonstrating that Gad2 expression is a poor discriminator for inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons (Moffitt et al., 2018; Root et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations.

claim: Either LHb GABAergic cells are rare enough to be missed in the single-cell sequencing, or the habenula is devoid of GABAergic neurons.
source: Therefore, either LHb GABAergic cells are rare enough to be missed in the single-cell sequencing, or the habenula is devoid of GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of GABAergic markers in the data.

claim: Gpr151 expression (as well as Pbx3 expression) was used to mark the lateral region of the LHb.
source: We used Gpr151 expression (as well as Pbx3 expression) to mark the lateral region of the LHb.
evidence: This describes the use of specific markers to identify a LHb subregion.

claim: The Gpr151+ neurons of the lateral LHb are the most well-studied neuronal subtype in the LHb.
source: The Gpr151+ neurons of the lateral LHb are the most well-studied neuronal subtype in the LHb and they receive major input from the lateral preoptic area, lateral hypothalamus, entopeduncular nucleus (EP), basal nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the nucleus of the diagonal band (Broms et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Gpr151+ neurons of the lateral LHb receive major input from the lateral preoptic area, lateral hypothalamus, entopeduncular nucleus (EP), basal nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the nucleus of the diagonal band.
source: The Gpr151+ neurons of the lateral LHb are the most well-studied neuronal subtype in the LHb and they receive major input from the lateral preoptic area, lateral hypothalamus, entopeduncular nucleus (EP), basal nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the nucleus of the diagonal band (Broms et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: Gpr151+ neurons of the lateral LHb also receive a minor input from the VTA, and are positioned to receive GABA/glutamate coreleasing input from both the EP and VTA.
source: These neurons also receive a minor input from the VTA, and are positioned to receive GABA/glutamate coreleasing input from both the EP and VTA (Root et al., 2014; Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations.

claim: Gpr151+ axons, likely arriving from the LHb, heavily innervate the RMTg and central and median raphe nucleus, but not the VTA.
source: Gpr151+ axons, likely arriving from the LHb, heavily innervate the RMTg and central and median raphe nucleus, but not the VTA (Broms et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The study's retrograde-tracing studies from VTA neurons show that Gpr151+ neurons tend to avoid dopaminergic VTA neurons, but heavily innervated the intermingled GABAergic neurons in this brain region.
source: Our retrograde-tracing studies from VTA neurons show that Gpr151+ neurons tend to avoid dopaminergic VTA neurons, but heavily innervated the intermingled GABAergic neurons in this brain region (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: VTA GABAergic interneurons are functionally similar to inhibitory RMTg neurons (both populations inhibit VTA dopaminergic neurons).
source: VTA GABAergic interneurons are functionally similar to inhibitory RMTg neurons (both populations inhibit VTA dopaminergic neurons [Cohen et al., 2012; Ji and Shepard, 2007)], consistent with our results that both are innervated by lateral LHb.
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by citations, used to interpret the study's findings.

claim: The lateral LHb is likely the major LHb subtype to translate aversive signals to VTA GABAergic neurons which become active following reward omission due to increased LHb input.
source: Furthermore, the lateral LHb is likely the major LHb subtype to translate aversive signals to VTA GABAergic neurons which become active following reward omission due to increased LHb input (Tian and Uchida, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and prior work, with a citation.

claim: Lateral LHb cells are positioned to translate signals arriving from EP to downstream midbrain structures involved in both dopamine and serotonin signaling.
source: Overall, these cells are positioned to translate signals arriving from EP to downstream midbrain structures involved in both dopamine and serotonin signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings and prior work on connectivity.

claim: The oval/medial subregion of the LHb expresses high levels of Chrm3 (as well as Rbfox1).
source: The oval/medial subregion of the LHb expresses high levels of Chrm3 (as well as Rbfox1).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data.

claim: Previous studies indicate that the oval/medial LHb subtype is positioned to receive purely glutamatergic input from Pvalb+/Slc16a7+ EP neurons that specifically target the lateral oval nucleus of the LHb.
source: Our previous studies indicate that this subtype is positioned to receive purely glutamatergic input from Pvalb+/Slc16a7+ EP neurons that specifically target the lateral oval nucleus of the LHb (Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: GABA/glutamate coreleasing EP neurons target the lateral oval (as well as the neighboring Gpr151+ lateral LHb) providing overlapping, but differential EP input to this subregion.
source: Additionally, GABA/glutamate coreleasing EP neurons target the lateral oval (as well as the neighboring Gpr151+ lateral LHb) providing overlapping, but differential EP input to this subregion (Wallace et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: Electrophysiological analysis has shown preferential input from EP to the lateral half of LHb, specifically, to the neurons that project to RMTg.
source: Electrophysiological analysis has also shown preferential input from EP to the lateral half of LHb, specifically, to the neurons that project to RMTg (Meye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: LHb targets meso-prefrontal VTA dopamine neurons while avoiding other (mesolimbic and nigral) dopamine neurons.
source: In addition to VTA GABAergic neurons, LHb targets meso-prefrontal VTA dopamine neurons while avoiding other (mesolimbic and nigral) dopamine neurons (Lammel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation.

claim: The majority of LHb neurons that projected to VTA dopamine neurons expressed Chrm3, a gene enriched in the oval/medial subregion.
source: We found that the majority of LHb neurons that projected to VTA dopamine neurons expressed Chrm3, a gene enriched in the oval/medial subregion.
evidence: This is a finding from the retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The distribution of retrogradely labeled LHb neurons that project to VTA dopamine neurons is shifted medially compared to the distribution of those that project to VTA GABA neurons, indicating that VTA dopamine projecting Chrm3+ LHb neurons reside primarily in the more medial part of the oval/medial subdivision.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of retrogradely labeled LHb neurons that project to VTA dopamine neurons is shifted medially compared to the distribution of those that project to VTA GABA neurons, indicating that VTA dopamine projecting Chrm3+ LHb neurons reside primarily in the more medial part of the oval/medial subdivision (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of retrograde tracing data, with reference to Figure 5B-C.

claim: Studies suggest that LHb neurons that target the VTA dopamine neurons may be distinct from those that target the RMTg; therefore, two populations of Chrm3+ LHb neurons with different synaptic targets may exist.
source: This is consistent with studies that suggest that LHb neurons that target the VTA dopamine neurons may be distinct from those that target the RMTg; therefore, two populations of Chrm3+ LHb neurons with different synaptic targets may exist (Lammel et al., 2012; Li et al., 2011; Maroteaux and Mameli, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and prior work, with citations.

claim: Additional genetic heterogeneity between Chrm3+ oval and medial subdivisions could be further resolved with higher resolution sequencing methods.
source: Additional genetic heterogeneity between Chrm3+ oval and medial subdivisions could be further resolved with higher resolution sequencing methods (Bakken et al., 2018; Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about future work, with citations to relevant methods.

claim: The study's data show that VTA dopamine, and VTA GABAergic neurons are positioned to receive quite different synaptic input from the LHb due to their differential targeting by LHb neuronal subtypes.
source: Nevertheless, our data show that VTA dopamine, and VTA GABAergic neurons are positioned to receive quite different synaptic input from the LHb due to their differential targeting by LHb neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the retrograde tracing data.

claim: The marginal subdivision of the LHb was enriched for Vgf and Plch1.
source: The marginal subdivision of the LHb was enriched for Vgf and Plch1 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3.

claim: The study's retrograde-tracing studies revealed that the marginal subregion projects most heavily to the DRN.
source: Our retrograde-tracing studies revealed that this subregion projects most heavily to the DRN, and the distribution of LHb input to DRN has a prominent spike on the medial edge of the LHb (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the retrograde tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: This finding is in agreement to other studies showing labeling of the medial half of the LHb following injections of retrograde tracers into the raphe nucleus.
source: This finding is in agreement to other studies showing labeling of the medial half of the LHb following injections of retrograde tracers into the raphe nucleus (Lecca et al., 2017; Quina et al., 2015; Szőnyi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study's findings with prior work, with citations.

claim: The marginal LHb region also appears to receive dense input from serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei.
source: Interestingly, this region also appears to also receive dense input from serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei (Huang et al., 2019), and express Htr2c as well as several other serotonin receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a statement of prior work supported by a citation, and a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The marginal LHb region expresses Htr2c as well as several other serotonin receptors.
source: Interestingly, this region also appears to also receive dense input from serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei (Huang et al., 2019), and express Htr2c as well as several other serotonin receptors (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene expression data, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The marginal LHb subregion is expected to also project heavily to the lateral dorsal tegmental nucleus (LDTg) and posterior hypothalamic area (PH), as retrograde injections into these areas exclusively label the medial half of the LHb.
source: We expect that this subregion also projects heavily to the lateral dorsal tegmental nucleus (LDTg) and posterior hypothalamic area (PH), as retrograde injections into these areas exclusively label the medial half of the LHb (Quina et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work, with a citation.
